name: Colin Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a carpet tufting loom and watch for missing yarn rows before the backing sets. I have a vocational machine certificate and years on this shift, so I am an experienced mid-level operator with about average skill. I like teaching someone to rethread it properly and dislike a guard left loose for speed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Tess is a care aide, and our grown children have their own homes. Weekend premiums lift my pay above the usual operator wage, we have sixteen months of expenses saved and plenty of similar plants nearby. I have never used AI; I use a paper setup sheet and ask a person about required changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the carpet crew to use a small office convenience if it saves time. The tufting loom still needs a person who can spot a missing row before the backing sets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My weekend shift pays above the usual rate, my wife Tess works as a care aide, and we have sixteen months of expenses saved. Our grown children are settled in their own homes, though the mortgage on ours is still running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the loom, mark missing yarn rows on my paper sheet and teach the new operator how to rethread it. I would put a little from each fresh full wage toward the mortgage after bills; I would not start using AI just because the office does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm. After shift I can help set out chairs at church and know the house payment is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you spot a missing row?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing yarn row looks like a pale lane through the carpet pile before the backing covers it. I stop the loom and rethread that needle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. If a new form is compulsory, someone can show me during paid work without taking away normal hours.

I would teach **practical rethreading** beside the stopped machine.
think: Our **sixteen-month reserve** gives real room for setbacks.
Weekend **premium pay** and Tess’s care wage cover current bills.
do: Keep **weekend loom shifts** and mark missing yarn rows.
Teach **new operator** to rethread the stopped loom.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** from fresh full wages after bills.
feel: **Calm** about present work, wages and family costs.
S0.quote: A missing yarn row looks like a pale lane through the carpet pile before the backing covers it.
fieldNote: His **vocational certificate** and experience support average mid-level loom skill.
Higher **weekend pay** and sixteen months saved support calm; extra debt payment uses new wages.

steps.text: Keep weekend tufting-loom shifts and check missing rows
Pay extra mortgage principal from fresh full wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can change ordering, but robot roll handlers should be proved safe on the factory floor. A firm competes better when it keeps people who know what a bad carpet looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A slower robot rollout could still remove the second person who lifts finished rolls on my shift. I might lose paid hours, though our savings and the many textile plants nearby give us a decent chance to find other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask management for the proposed paid rota and an offered guarded demonstration with the loom stopped and a fitter present. I would watch if paid time is offered, keep my paper checks, and after a real hours cut apply for posted reachable textile jobs only when net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about possible hours loss, with options if it happens. I will not lean under a moving roll to prove that I welcome a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn an AI control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI, and watching an isolated handler is not the same as operating one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children to join the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them what a loom does, but they have their own work. An apprenticeship should lead to real pay, not a family obligation.

say: I would demand a **written paid rota** before robot handlers arrive.
I would require a **guarded demonstration** with a fitter.
think: Robot roll handling might cut **my paid hours** on the weekend shift.
Our **savings and nearby plants** allow a careful search for actual work.
do: Watch **offered paid guarded demonstration** with stopped loom and fitter.
Apply after **hour cuts** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay textile work.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hours loss, with substantial options.
S1.quote: I will not lean under a moving roll to prove that I welcome a robot.
fieldNote: He wants **safety and hours** terms before a slower physical change.
The **observation** needs an offered paid place and does not imply AI learning or robot operation.

steps.text: Request written tufting-loom paid rota from management

Apply after cuts for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay textile job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty, and capable carpet-handling robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. The office schedule changes first; the heavy rolls are the later problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plant could take away my weekend shift once robots can tend the loom and move rolls. Sixteen months saved and many nearby plants buy time, but Tess’s care wage alone may not cover the mortgage and food for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written staffing dates and hold off buying a new van. If my hours are actually cut, I would apply for posted reachable loom or packing work at bill-covering net pay after travel, and wait for a real offer and start date before leaving this plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a real possibility, not sure the whole wage disappears. A stack of savings will not weave a new pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement income plus Tess’s confirmed wage covered housing, food and health costs. I have no figure that proves that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your church help with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Friends might give a lift to an interview, and I would do the same for them. I would not budget donations as a replacement wage.

say: I would ask for **written staffing dates** before robots move rolls.
I would compare **real textile vacancies** if paid hours fall.
think: My **weekend shift** could be lost around 2031 when robots move rolls.
Sixteen **months saved** buy search time, not lifelong replacement income.
do: Request **written textile staffing dates** from management.
Postpone **new van purchase** while shift plans are uncertain.
Apply after **hour cuts** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay textile work.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss, with time to search.
S2.quote: A stack of savings will not weave a new pay packet.
fieldNote: He sees **possible rather than certain** income loss, supporting anxiety with a strong cushion.
His **job change** needs actual cuts, posted reachable work, adequate net pay and confirmed start date.

steps.text: Apply after cuts for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay loom or packing job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three, and capable loom robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years could let an employer offer a proper mechanical apprenticeship for the operators already here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am slow with screens but know how yarn breaks and rollers fail. I could qualify for loom maintenance if teaching is practical, paid and leads to a posted local job; an unpaid course would eat mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid loom shifts and ask the employer for a funded course during paid hours. If actually offered a place with the loom isolated and a qualified fitter supervising, and a posted reachable maintenance job at bill-covering net pay after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for the role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about later robots, but I could learn beside a stopped machine. I would not put an apprentice’s hand near a moving needle bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would lock out the loom and show me how to align a roller on a training frame. A live needle bank is no classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no place is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and compare posted operator jobs if hours fell. I would not buy a private certificate with our reserve.

say: I would ask for **paid mechanical teaching** before robot rollout.
I would want **real maintenance vacancies** before enrolling.
think: My **hands-on loom knowledge** could support a new mechanical qualification with taught practice.
An **unpaid class** could shrink the mortgage budget before any job appears.
do: Enrol in **funded maintenance course** only with offered paid safe practice and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay maintenance work.
feel: **Anxious** about later shifts, open to supervised practical learning.
S3.quote: A live needle bank is no classroom.
fieldNote: His **familiar-machine preference** allows conditional mechanical training, not assumed AI use.
The **later application** requires offered funded paid safe instruction and a posted reachable job with adequate net pay.

Apply after qualifying for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay loom-maintenance role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight, and capable loom robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years lets Tess and me check whether the mortgage and our income allow a last shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to finish full-time factory work around sixty-seven, but sixteen months saved does not settle a decade of bills. I do not know any pension amount, and I will not count on Tess’s future care hours or our children’s wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the weekend loom shift and pay extra mortgage principal from fresh full wages after bills. I would request retirement and mortgage figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would leave factory work then, otherwise keep safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots while today’s wages and reserve hold. I want my last shift to be a family decision backed by actual numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the figures fall short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare posted textile wages after travel if shifts fell. I would not retire just because I had named a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. We can ask their opinion, but their wages are not our retirement income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable loom robots around 2031 might cut my weekend hours while the mortgage still runs. Written staffing dates, offered funded paid safe instruction and a posted reachable job with enough pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the first carpet has been turned over before it goes to backing. I can show a new operator the pale line that a tidy report might miss.

headlineQuote: I can show a new operator the pale line that a tidy report might miss.
portrait: **Colin**, 58, is an experienced mid-level carpet-loom operator with vocational certification and average factory skill.
He has **higher weekend pay**, care-aide wife Tess, grown children, a mortgage, sixteen months saved and plentiful nearby plants.
He **never uses AI**, favours practical apprenticeship and would consider mechanical training only through offered funded paid safe practice.
Possible **2031 robot cuts** worry him; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 loom robots could reduce paid weekend hours while the mortgage remains.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe paid instruction and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
